newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya's Moi signals that coffee auctions to stay.
newsitem.headline: Kenya's Moi signals that coffee auctions to stay.

text.p: Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi signalled that Kenya's coffee export auction system will remain unchanged despite pressure for a bigger role by millers.

Moi told a public rally in the key coffee growing Nyeri town that all matters related to coffee marketing must remain the domain of the Coffee Board of Kenya (CBK) and even the ministry of agriculture must not interfere with that.
"Coffee marketing is the work of the board. They know what must be done for the industry," Moi told cheering farmers.

That put to temporary rest a debate on the future of coffee marketing in Kenya. Millers, led by the Kenya Planters' Cooperative Union and the commercial Thika Coffee Mills had led a campaign to share CBK's role as marketing bodies.

Under Kenyan laws, millers and producers must surrender their coffee to the board for sale at the weekly export auction. Under reforms by the board, millers and others can then buy back their coffee at auction for their clients.
The millers say it it ridiculous they should surrender their coffee to the board only to repurchase at the auction and want to be allowed to sell directly to roasters.
The board rejects any shift from the status quo and the Sunday Nation newspaper, in an editorial, fully backed the coffee board position on export auctions.
"Basically, the complaint appears to be that whereas Kenya coffee has always been sold at open auction, the milling sharks are out to set up a regime of private-treaty deals.

"Old hands in the industry insist that there is no better guarantee for a fair price and one reflective of world market realities as far as the smallholder is concerned than the open auction system," the Sunday Nation said.

"They warn of an overwhelming lack of transparency and accountability in private treaty deals and point out that the government, too, would find the arrangement highly inconvenient from the point of view of revenue collection and keeping track of commissions and other payments for taxation purposes."

"The upshot of this is that total coffee pricing would be severely depressed, there would be no buying on the open market and smallholders with little or no knowledge of world market dynamics would be tricked," the newspaper added.

Last week, Moi appeared to signal a marketing change, saying millers would be allowed a more influential marketing role provided they raised one billion shillings ($18 million) as bail protection against and farmer losses/
But that idea appeared to have been scuttled by his latest instructions, which a coffee board spokesman said reflected the government's "true position on the coffee industry as of now".
